name: Renulife violet ray

lead: Violet rays were early 20th-century electrotherapy devices that delivered high-voltage, high-frequency, low-current discharges through glass electrodes. Renulife was one of the major US makers, alongside Fitzgerald and Fisher, and Master Electric was the last US manufacturer.

Promoters claimed they treated everything from lower back pain to carbuncles, and a c. 1920 manual recommended them for brain fog and catarrh. Users applied them to the scalp and skin in the hope of better circulation, hair and complexion.

paras: A control box with an interrupter and magneto coil connected to a handle with interchangeable glass electrodes, which was passed over the body or scalp. Many vintage units survive with collectors.

US authorities took action against makers in the 1940s and 1950s, including seizures and destruction orders; Master Electric devices were seized in 1951. High-voltage devices can cause burns and shocks.

lead: Violet rays were electrotherapy devices of the early twentieth century that produced high-voltage, high-frequency, low-current discharges. A control box held the interrupter and magneto coil, and a handle held the high-voltage coil and interchangeable glass electrodes.[1] Renulife, Fitzgerald and Fisher were among the major US makers, and most US units were made before the Depression.[1]

Promoters said the devices could treat conditions from lower back pain to carbuncles; Edgar Cayce advocated them in almost 900 readings.[1] In the 1940s and 1950s makers faced lawsuits, recalls, seizures and destruction orders, and in 1951 the FDA seized Master Electric devices after a lawsuit in Marion, Indiana.[1]
infobox: FDA seizure of Master Electric devices, 1951[1]

paras: The handle held a high-voltage coil and the electrodes were interchangeable glass attachments.[1]

Wikipedia notes a claim, flagged as lacking a citation, that Nikola Tesla's first prototype was shown at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition.[1] Many manufacturers stopped during World War II, switching to radio coils and other war components, and Master Electric was the last US maker.[1]
Government actions in the 1940s and 1950s included recalls, seizures, forfeitures and destruction orders; later case law is described as prohibiting their manufacture in the US.[1]
Since the 1990s, similar devices called violet wands have been marketed for other forms of electrostimulation.[1]
